Abstract A proposed initiated constitutional amendment in Ohio would prohibit all taxes on real property, eliminating an estimated $21.1 billion in revenue for the state’s schools and municipalities. If voters approve the measure, state lawmakers would only have one year to adopt replacement revenue mechanisms and establish formulas for allocating the offsetting revenue. This paper estimates state-level rate increases necessary to offset the loss of property tax revenue under both individual income and general sales taxes, evaluates options for allocating that replacement revenue, and examines the economic and distributional consequences of such a tax shift. Full revenue replacement under the central scenario would require an 8.24 percent flat state-level individual income tax, yielding a 10.29 percent combined state and local flat rate. Three graduated-rate income tax alternatives are also considered, all producing top state-level rates above 12 percent under central assumptions. An offsetting increase in the general sales tax would require a 13.36 percent state rate, for an average combined state and local rate of 14.53 percent. Whatever replacement option is selected, both the new revenue instrument and the means of revenue allocation will necessarily yield substantial divergence from current tax distributions, often involving a substantial shift in resources from urban to rural counties, or vice versa. Keywords: Property Tax Repeal; Tax Revolts; Property Taxation; Ohio Property Tax; Tax Swaps

1 Replacing the Irreplaceable: Analyzing Revenue Alternatives for Ohio Property Taxes Executive Summary A proposed initiated constitutional amendment in Ohio would prohibit any future taxes on real property, creating a $21 billion budget hole for Ohio’s schools and local governments. The measure does not specify any revenue replacement mechanism, leaving that consequential task to the state legislature. This paper estimates the increases in individual income and sales tax rates required to offset the loss of real property tax revenue, evaluates a range of possible mechanisms for allocating replacement revenue to political subdivisions, and analyzes the economic and distributional consequences of these potential tax swaps. Local income and sales tax bases vary too widely for local-level tax replacement to be viable. Realistically, replacement revenue must be generated at the state level and then allocated back to schools, counties, municipalities, and special districts. The paper begins by defining the revenue gap resulting from the repeal of real property taxes, adjusting for existing state offsets like rollback credits and the homestead exemption.1 The paper then identifies possible state-level revenue replacement options. A single-rate (flat) income tax and three graduated-rate structures are considered. Revenue replacement would require a flat state rate of 8.24 percent, up from 2.75 percent, and top rates under the three example graduated rate structures would all exceed 12 percent, with the most highly progressive plan requiring a top rate of 22.32 percent. Rates are calculated with and without Ohio’s Business Income Deduction, which exempts the first $250,000 in pass-through business income. Ohio’s existing municipal income taxes, which average 2.05 percent, would sit atop these state rates. Under sales tax replacement, the state rate would have to increase to 13.36 percent, yielding a combined state-local rate of 14.53 percent. Such extraordinarily high rates would drive significant taxpayer responses. Consumers could respond to high sales tax rates with increased cross-border shopping, while higher income taxes could drive residents entirely out of state. Raising replacement revenue is only half the challenge facing policymakers if voters ban real property taxes. Lawmakers must also determine how to allocate the alternative revenue to local governments. In the absence of property taxes, continued assessments lack justification and would generate perverse incentives if retained, since local governing bodies would benefit from inflated valuations without those faulty valuations imposing costs on local property owners. State officials would be forced to find another way to allocate revenue to school districts, counties, municipalities, and special districts. This paper considers three possible options: replacing final-year property tax collections for each jurisdiction, with an annual adjustment for inflation and population growth; per capita allocation; 1 Real property tax collected under fixed-sum levies is treated as requiring replacement even though, mechanically, rates would increase to generate the same amount of revenue from the residual utility tangible personal property within the fixed-sum levy base, since absorption requires an implausible seventeen-fold increase in taxes on utilities.

# Page 6^page=6
2 and a needs-based approach, modeled here through a school funding proxy. Each approach has substantial limitations. If the state locks in prior collections, it forever subsidizes formerly higher-tax jurisdictions at the expense of lower-tax communities. Other approaches generate dramatic shortfalls and windfalls, depending on the jurisdiction. All approaches are inflexible, unable to respond to new investment or changing economic conditions. Fundamentally, moreover, any state-level replacement eliminates local accountability, severing the connection between local taxation and local services. Distributionally, any replacement revenue option will exhibit substantial economic variance from current property tax collections. Many individuals, and (collectively) many jurisdictions, will pay far more under an income or sales tax increase than they save in property taxes, while others will receive substantial tax relief. To illustrate this effect, the paper examines the net effect of replacement options for rural, suburban, and urban counties in aggregate, with county-by-county calculations in the appendix. Under a single-rate income tax, Ohio’s urban counties would pay 6.8 percent less in aggregate, while net tax burdens in suburban and small metro counties would increase by 3.1 percent, and rural counties’ tax burden would rise by 7.6 percent. Under the most progressive graduated rate income tax considered, urban counties’ net tax burdens would decline by 12.2 percent while rural counties would experience a 19.1 percent net tax increase. These rural jurisdictions typically had relatively low property tax burdens, and their additional income tax burdens would subsidize higher replacement levels elsewhere. Sales tax effects would be even more dramatic, with a 10.3 percent reduction in urban counties’ burdens and a 25.9 percent increase in rural counties’ net tax burdens. The paper proceeds with sample taxpayer calculations, showing that under income tax replacement scenarios, most middle-class households would face higher tax liability than under the current system. It also examines the literature on the economic ramifications of tax swaps, noting that property taxes are more economically efficient than income or sales taxes. This means that a dramatic shift away from property taxes toward much heavier income or sales tax burdens would undercut Ohio’s economic growth. The property tax’s efficiency is reinforced by the benefit principle of taxation. Local services confer benefits on local property roughly in proportion to value, making the property tax less like a traditional tax and more akin to a fee for services, at least relative to income or sales taxes, which have no connection to property value or services to property. Additionally, because future property tax liability is partially capitalized into home prices, property tax repeal would raise entry prices for prospective homebuyers. The paper concludes with five challenges that replacement efforts must confront: (1) any replacement will dramatically change the distribution of tax burdens; (2) allocation options also yield substantial variations; (3) tax burdens would no longer be commensurate with local spending or responsive to local preferences; (4) revenue offsets would be less economically efficient than the current system; and (5) policymakers would have relatively little time to design and implement a replacement system.

3 Introduction Ohio’s schools, counties, municipalities, and special districts will collectively generate more than $21 billion in revenue from real property taxes—or possibly $0. A proposed initiated constitutional amendment (Abolishment of Taxes on Real Property 2025) would prohibit any taxes on real property, effective the first day of the year after its ratification. While the measure failed to obtain enough signatures to appear on the 2026 ballot, signature collection is ongoing to place it on the 2027 ballot. If voters approve it by a simple majority vote in November of 2027, Ohio’s political subdivisions would lose the tax responsible for nearly two-thirds of their tax revenue, and about a quarter of all revenue, for the 2028 tax year (payable in 2029).2 Should voters approve the measure, Ohio’s legislature would face one of the most daunting fiscal challenges ever confronted by state lawmakers when it convenes the following January: how to offset the loss of the single largest source of revenue in Ohio’s state and local tax system, and how to allocate any replacement revenue to the local governing bodies stripped of this taxing authority, in the space of one year. The magnitude of the challenge defies ready solutions, and the easiest course of action is inertia, premised on the assumption that voters will not approve property tax abolition without a replacement mechanism in place. But without an assessment of the alternatives, any evaluation of the proposal is necessarily incomplete and based on inadequate information. This paper explores Ohio’s options for replacing local property tax revenue in the event of that tax’s repeal, with estimates of the necessary offsetting rates under both individual income and general sales taxes. It also analyzes several possible mechanisms for allocating this revenue and considers their implications for local finance, and examines the broader economic ramifications of replacing the property tax. We find that full replacement under standard assumptions would require an 8.24 percent flat state-level individual income tax (compared to a current 2.75 percent flat rate), with an average state and local combined rate of 10.29 percent once accounting for existing school and municipal income taxes. Replacement using higher sales tax rates would necessitate a 13.36 percent state- level sales tax (compared to 5.75 percent under current law) with an average state and local combined sales tax rate of 14.53 percent. Three potential graduated-rate income tax structures are also considered, all yielding top state-level rates in excess of 12 percent. Distributional effects differ based on the parameters of replacement taxes, but all alternatives yield substantial divergence from current geographic tax distributions and generate stark urban-rural divides. 2 The text of the proposed amendment is slightly ambiguous on timing, stipulating that “[N]o real property shall be taxed,” to take effect the first day of the year after passage (i.e., January 1, 2028). Property taxes are paid in arrears, and state officials have interpreted this to mean that no additional liability would attach as of 2028, but that taxpayers would still remit property taxes in 2028 based on 2027 liability. We adopt this interpretation as well.

4 Defining the Revenue Gap Ohio’s $21 Billion Budget Hole Ohio’s political subdivisions levied $25.22 billion in property taxes in tax year 2025, of which $22.62 billion was derived from taxes on real property (Ohio Department of Taxation [ODT] 2026c). For tax year 2027, the Ohio Legislative Service Commission estimates $23.17 billion from taxes on real property (2025), and we project that Ohio’s residual tangible personal property (TPP) tax, which only applies to public utility property, will generate an additional $2.7 billion. Tangible personal property taxes are not prohibited by the proposed constitutional amendment and can be presumed to remain in place, even though maintaining property tax administration solely for levies on utility tangible property is peculiar and inefficient. Notably, about $2.7 billion of Ohio’s real property tax collections derive from fixed-sum levies where mills are automatically adjusted to raise a specified amount each year.3 Fixed-sum levies include bond, debt, emergency, substitute, and sinking-fund levies, and these levies apply to tangible as well as real property. We estimate the current utility TPP fixed-sum levy tax burden at $162.1 million. If real property taxes were repealed, however, only utility TPP would remain in the fixed-sum levy bases. Rates on utility property within these levies would have to rise seventeen-fold to generate the same revenue, and total statewide taxes on TPP would nearly double. Because it seems implausible that state lawmakers would wish to permit a seventeen-fold increase in utility tangible property taxes in economically distressed school districts, much of which could be passed along to utility ratepayers, we assume arguendo that the fixed-sum levy share of the real property tax burden would have to be replaced as well rather than being shifted to this narrow TPP class, though this is not technically obligatory under the proposed amendment. Ohio currently provides two rollback credits and a homestead exemption as offsets to property tax liability (ODT 2025b). This relief is funded by the state, and we estimate the value of this relief at $2.03 billion for tax year 2027. In the absence of the property tax, lawmakers would need to adjust the existing mechanisms to redirect this aid to affected local governments. Nevertheless, it provides existing capacity for a partial offset, leaving a $21.14 billion hole for lawmakers to fill if voters repeal the property tax. This amount—approximately $4,244 per household—is about 83 percent of what the state currently collects in state-level income and sales taxes combined (Ohio Office of Management and Budget 2026). Lawmakers could, of course, elect not to replace the entire property tax, permitting some degree of “haircut” for school districts and municipalities. The following analysis assumes full revenue replacement, but readers may choose to apply discounts to reported values to the degree that they believe overall local revenue reductions viable or desirable. 3 That Ohio’s utility TPP tax revenue and its fixed-sum levy revenue are both approximately $2.7 billion is merely coincidental. Only a small share of fixed-sum levy revenue currently derives from utility TPP, though this would change if real property taxes were repealed and lawmakers did not adopt some adjustment to the current fixed-sum levy system.

5 Fixed-Sum Levies This analysis assumes that real property tax revenue within fixed-sum levies will have to be replaced at the state level, rather than permitting utility tangible property within these levies to be taxed at rates sufficient to offset the loss of real property from the base. We did, however, calculate the county-level implications of the resulting TPP tax increases if lawmakers failed to address this issue. These calculations were accomplished using Ohio levy-by-levy rate data (ODT 2026e), district- level abstracts of real and tangible property (ODT 2026a), and county-level gross levy data (ODT 2026c). Fixed-sum levies were identified by levy purpose,4 permitting an estimated fixed- sum share of each district’s tax rate. This share was applied to tax amounts in district tax abstracts, yielding estimates of the portion of public utility TPP taxes attributable to fixed-sum levies and the total fixed-sum levy dollars raised in each district, which were then aggregated at the county level. We estimate that utility TPP raises $162.1 million of the $2.67 billion generated by fixed-sum levies. Statewide, utility TPP taxes within these levies would have to be 16.4 times current levels to meet the fixed-sum amount, with county-level increases topping out at 43.2 times current levels in Mercer County. The result would be a near-doubling of current utility TPP taxes statewide, including both ordinary and fixed-sum levies, with dramatic regional variation. A table showing county-aggregated multipliers can be found in the appendix. Identifying Revenue Replacement Options Ohio’s property taxes are local taxes, but any revenue replacement effort would almost certainly have to proceed at the state level. While state legislators could conceivably authorize sufficient additional local income or sales tax authority to permit local-level replacement, variations in income and sales tax bases across municipalities and school districts are too large for this approach to be viable. According to a prior analysis exploring the necessary countywide aggregate rates, inclusive of both existing and newly required school, county, and municipal income taxes, the required local rates ranged from an additional 7.00 percent in Geauga County (atop the 2.75 percent state rate) to 24.26 percent in Harrison County (Walczak 2025). Replacement with local sales taxes would yield similarly extreme variations: jurisdictions with large retail concentrations would have much more reasonable rates relative to rural, low-income, or largely residential communities with a limited sales tax base. In this paper, therefore, we consider options for replacing lost property tax revenue with state-level increases in individual income taxes and general sales taxes. These initial estimates do not take any behavioral or other economic responses into account, even though some marginal response is inevitable. Although economists disagree about 4 We identified BOND, DEBT, SINK, SUBS, and EMER levies where levy files showed that standard tax reduction factors did not apply. 6 taxpayers’ responsiveness to tax increases, there is a general consensus that property taxes create fewer economic distortions than do other major taxes, suggesting—as will be considered later— that a shift to other taxes would reduce overall economic output. Some taxpayers may also relocate in response to higher income taxes, even if their overall tax burden does not change. They may be particularly motivated to move if changes in tax distributions yield substantially higher total tax liability without any commensurate increase in (and potentially even a diminution of) local school and municipal budgets. Consumers may also respond to high sales tax rates with increased cross-border shopping. For these reasons, all rate estimates should be regarded as a lower bound. Actual rates would likely have to be higher to account for taxpayer responses. Individual Income Tax Under recently adopted reforms, Ohio levies a single-rate income tax at a rate of 2.75 percent above its zero-tax threshold, currently $26,050. Pass-through business income is taxed at a higher rate of 3.0 percent, though sole proprietorships and pass-through businesses are eligible for the Business Income Deduction (BID), a deduction for the first $250,000 in pass-through business income (R.C. §§ 5747.01(A)(28), 5747.02(4)(a)). The 3 percent pass-through rate was originally adopted under Ohio’s former graduated-rate income tax and represented a preferential rather than a higher rate, though with the BID in place, the current system still benefits pass- through businesses with up to $3 million in income. Ohio also offers a joint filer tax credit. The credit was originally designed to counteract the marriage penalty under a graduated-rate system that did not double bracket widths for joint filers, and is now retained to provide a similar offset for the zero-bracket. The current maximum credit of $650, which is phased out for high earners, eliminates most of the marriage penalty from not doubling the zero-bracket from $26,050 to $52,100 for eligible joint filers. For estimates involving a single-rate tax, we leave this system unaltered, with an identical zero-bracket and joint filer credit. In modeling hypothetical graduated-rate income tax options, we consider tax schedules with and without a marriage penalty. These replacements assume doubling of bracket widths in lieu of a substantially reworked joint filer credit for marriage penalty elimination. Ohio’s school districts and municipalities impose income taxes as well. Using the most recent available data (ODT 2025a; 2025c; 2026b), we calculate a weighted average local income tax rate of 2.06 percent. Such heavy reliance on local income taxation is relatively unusual, as is the number of governmental units with such taxing authority. Ohio and neighboring Pennsylvania together account for three-quarters of all local income taxing authorities in the country (Walczak et al. 2023). Single-Rate Income Tax If Ohio abolished the business income deduction and the differential treatment of business and non-business income, we estimate that the state’s flat rate would need to increase from 2.75 percent to 7.80 percent to offset the loss of local property tax revenue. The combined average state and local income tax rate would be 9.86 percent. The relative increase in income taxes for

7 sole proprietors and other pass-through business owners would be even greater than for other income taxpayers in this scenario. Our central assumption involves retaining the $250,000 business income deduction while applying the same rate to all taxable business and non-business income. This yields a replacement rate of 8.24 percent, for a 10.29 percent combined state and local rate. Finally, if lawmakers wished to retain the current treatment of business income, restoring the provision’s original preferential intent, a retained BID and an alternative 3 percent rate on taxable business income would require a 10.28 percent state rate and 12.33 percent combined rate on non-business income. This approach would shield small businesses from dramatic rate increases, somewhat reducing adverse effects on employment and economic growth, though at the cost of even higher taxes on wage earners. While this scenario appears the least plausible, it is worth noting that Ohio also imposes the Corporate Activity Tax (CAT), a gross receipts tax that applies to pass-through business income, providing justification for some offset within the individual income tax. Fifteen states currently impose single-rate income taxes, with rates ranging from 2.5 percent in Arizona to 5.3 percent in Idaho. The median flat rate is 3.99 percent, and the unweighted average is 3.88 percent. Six of these fifteen states, including Ohio, permit political subdivisions to impose their own income taxes, with Philadelphia and Detroit featuring the highest all-in flat rates at 6.81 and 6.65 percent respectively. No jurisdiction in the country comes close to the double-digit combined rates necessary if Ohio replaced real property taxes with a high flat-rate tax. Graduated-Rate Income Tax A combined flat rate of 10.29 percent (in our central scenario) may be untenable, prompting lawmakers to consider reversing the policy reforms of recent years and reintroducing a graduated-rate tax. Lawmakers’ choice of possible rate schedules is virtually infinite, but a few hypothetical schedules may suffice to facilitate the evaluation of graduated-rate income taxes as an option. We consider three options: (1) replicating Ohio’s brackets and rate differentials as of 2019, before the most dramatic rounds of consolidation; (2) adopting the District of Columbia’s rates and brackets, lightly modified to maintain Ohio’s zero-bracket; and (3) implementing brackets based on those proposed by Ohio Rep. Tristan Rader. In each case, initial rates are adjusted

General Sales Tax Ohio’s 5.75 percent state sales tax rate is supplemented by “permissive share” county sales tax rates of 0.5 to 2.0 percent, with a statewide average local rate of 1.16 percent (ODT 2026d). The combined average rate of 6.91 percent is slightly below the average rate nationwide, though higher than the rates of most of Ohio’s neighbors. Replacing real property taxes with the sales tax would require a rate increase of 7.61 percent, yielding a state rate of 13.36 percent and a combined average rate of 14.53 percent. According to Tax Foundation estimates, the current highest statewide average combined rate is in Louisiana, at 10.11 percent, followed by Tennessee, which forgoes an individual income tax, at 9.61 percent (Mandal 2026). Under current county rates, Ohio’s highest resulting combined rate would be 15.36 percent, and the state rate alone would exceed the existing combined rate in any jurisdiction in the country. Rates at these levels are likely to induce cross-border shopping as a tax avoidance mechanism. Legally, Ohio consumers are obligated to remit use tax on the difference between another state’s sales tax rate and Ohio’s rate on products purchased elsewhere that are stored, used, consumed, or otherwise come to rest in Ohio. In practice, however, use compliance is extremely low for personal consumption, and state officials would be hard-pressed to enforce the use tax against a rise in cross-border purchases.

# Page 15^page=15
11 Designing Revenue Backfill Mechanisms Raising the necessary revenue is only half the equation for state lawmakers. They must also identify an equitable and administrable way to allocate that revenue to political subdivisions. Property rolls would cease to be a viable option, as there would be little justification for continued assessments in the absence of a property tax levy. Local governing bodies, moreover, would face peculiar incentives if they continued to assess properties for purposes of allocating state revenue transfers, since inflated assessments would only benefit the jurisdiction and local property owners would no longer have any incentive to guard against overassessment. Geographic estimates throughout this paper are based on statutory tax collections and resident income tax liability, and not a full economic incidence model. They show where taxes are legally remitted and where resident income tax liability or consumer sales tax liability arise, rather than fully allocating burdens to property owners, income earners, consumers, investors, or workers. Policy Challenges Associated with Revenue Backfill All options for allocating replacement revenue have meaningful shortcomings. The most intuitive approach, designed to avoid dramatic revenue swings, would be to replace final-year property tax collections, and adjust future transfers for inflation and population growth. Alternatively, policymakers could allocate revenue on a per capita basis, or according to a needs- based formula, though both approaches will yield sharp discontinuities with current receipts, with some jurisdictions claiming unexpected windfalls while others experience revenue contractions inconsistent with their existing financial obligations. If lawmakers seek to replace property tax revenue at existing levels, they lock in the effect of current mill levies even though the corresponding tax burden would no longer be borne by local taxpayers. Residents of jurisdictions that formerly imposed high property taxes would effectively be subsidized by other taxpayers across the state. They would enjoy perpetually higher resourcing than other jurisdictions, entirely divorced from local tax receipts. Some proposals elsewhere, including a failed North Dakota ballot measure (North Dakota Initiated Measure 4 2024), would have backfilled each jurisdiction’s final-year revenue figure in perpetuity, with no inflation or population adjustment. In addition to the erosion of the real value of the transfers due to inflation, this creates a perverse incentive for economic contraction. Population growth reduces revenue per capita, while shrinking communities experience an increase in per capita revenue. Local officials and homeowners are incentivized to reject new development, discourage business investment, and restrict population growth, all of which stretch revenues thin. Under this approach, residents reap benefits from stagnation and experience economic dynamism as a cost. Even population adjustments are likely inadequate to eliminate this effect entirely, as some forms of growth and new development impose more costs than others, and pure per capita adjustments are indifferent to local nuances. Growth that requires new infrastructure and expanded services is difficult to account for by formula.

12 More fundamentally, state-level replacement of property taxes deprives schools and municipalities of local control. Property taxes fund services that are uniquely close to the voters. Evaluating Economic Ramifications of the Tax Swap A precipitous increase in assessed values in recent years, not always accompanied by countervailing mill levy reductions, has fueled a new property tax revolt, in Ohio and around the country (Walczak 2024). Policymakers can be sympathetic to concerns raised by aggrieved homeowners, and open to reforms without committing to something as dramatic as property tax abolition, with all its attendant challenges and economic consequences. Economists generally regard property taxes (particularly taxes on real property) as more economically efficient than other major taxes, meaning they have less effect on economic decision-making and smaller impacts on economic growth. Property taxes are also praised for their relative stability, particularly compared with the volatility of income taxation. Policymakers frequently balance these benefits with other considerations, and with varying degrees of prioritization. Lawmakers may also care, for instance, about the distribution of tax burdens, the fairness of taxing unrealized gains, the ability to export tax burdens, and other factors. Nevertheless, the prevalence of property taxes as a local government funding mechanism is not accidental, and the economic literature strongly suggests that abandoning real property taxes in favor of alternative tax levies would harm Ohio’s economy.

Conversely, income taxes create a wedge between earnings from labor or investment and after-tax returns, yielding less work, reduced savings, and lower capital formation than would otherwise occur. Historically, the economic literature has been divided among two competing analytical frameworks: the capital tax view, under which property taxes are conceptualized as a levy on the return to capital invested in real estate, and the benefit view, which regards property taxes as a charge for services provided to property. # Page 24^page=24
20 against alternative revenue sources, however, the benefit view is particularly relevant, and likely the most accurate frame in more developed areas (Oates and Fischel 2016). Local governments overwhelmingly fund services whose value is capitalized into local properties. Schools, roads, police and fire services, parks, sanitation infrastructure, and other local services confer benefits to property and increase the value of that property, and they do so in rough proportion to property value. While this alignment is imprecise, property taxation to fund local services better accords with what public finance scholars refer to as the benefit principle of taxation than any other broad-based revenue option. Not all local government spending is efficient, and taxpayers may disagree on the optimal level and mix of government-funded services, but since property tax revenues disproportionately fund services that directly benefit those taxpayers, the economic effects are less like those of a traditional tax and (at least relatively) more like a price for bundled services. Local taxpayers, moreover, are uniquely empowered to calibrate local government expenditures. While local governments can never be perfectly responsive to the preferences of all voters individually, local school districts and municipal governments can better align with local preferences than can state government, which must operate more monolithically. Shifting from the property tax to an alternative state-level tax reduces responsiveness to local preferences and eliminates the connection between local tax burdens and benefits received. The capitalization framework reinforces the case for property tax efficiency. When governments overtax or spend tax revenues inefficiently, this is capitalized into lower property values, something local governments are incentivized to avoid (even beyond political incentives) because it reduces the local tax base. When the bundle of taxes and services is more attractive, the base expands and jurisdictions obtain greater fiscal capacity or the politically attractive and potentially pro-growth opportunity to return some or all of the surplus to taxpayers in the form of lower mill levies. None of this persists if state government assumes responsibility for replacement revenue. Finally, since property taxes are at least partially capitalized into the market value of real estate (Oates 1969), the price of real property is lower than it would be otherwise, reflecting future tax liability. This reduces the up-front costs of homeownership, with homeowners effectively trading a lower acquisition cost for the recurring tax obligation. Eliminating property taxes provides a windfall for current owners, whose property values would appreciate, but increases the entry price for would-be homebuyers (Horton et al. 2024). This reduction in housing affordability would, moreover, be paired with increased income or sales taxes, which are not capitalized into purchase prices and reduce prospective buyer’s purchasing capacity.
